consensus_summary: Gospel primarily denotes the good news of salvation / God’s saving reign accomplished through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ (kerygma), received by faith; kingdom announcement, the four Gospels as literature, and other emphases are common or minority alternatives but not replacements of this core.
book_summary: The gospel of the kingdom identified as the renewed covenant and the law going forth from Zion.
consensus_core_identification: good news of salvation through Christ’s death and resurrection (or God’s saving reign in him)
book_core_identification: gospel of the kingdom as the renewed covenant and the law going forth from Zion
boundary_disagreement: Book omits the Christ-event (death for sins, burial, resurrection) as constitutive of the meaning and substitutes covenant renewal plus law from Zion; consensus treats the latter themes as possible background or kingdom emphases but keeps the apostolic kerygma as the non-negotiable core.
material_contradiction: Accepting the book’s identification requires rejecting the consensus primary referent (1 Cor 15-style kerygma) in favor of a different content (renewed covenant / law from Zion) for the same term in the same theological domain.
rationale: Consensus responses uniformly fix the minimum core on the good news of salvation via Christ’s death and resurrection (anchored in 1 Cor 15, Rom 1, Mark 1, etc.), treating kingdom language as a compatible alternative emphasis rather than a substitute. The book’s entry, while noting the common Christ-centered view, defines Gospel instead as “the gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.” This is not a narrowing or re-boundarying of the same referent but a replacement of the central identification; the two cores cannot both be the primary meaning of the same term. Overlap in “kingdom” vocabulary or shared OT texts does not erase the contradiction at the core.
strongest_objection: The printed citations (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) support reign, new-covenant, and law-from-Zion themes but do not establish them as the definition of “Gospel” over against the NT kerygmatic texts that the consensus and the book’s own common-view note treat as decisive.
